To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the best MRA cost-benefit ratios are obtained in patients with vascular malformative conditions, and that the best M/R concordance is obtained in patients with menkes disease.
MRA and MRI are concordant in approximately two thirds of pediatric cases, and that MRA is most helpful for patients with Menkes disease, vascular malformation, and sickle-cell disease.

MRA was abnormal and concordant with MRI findings in children with Menkes' syndrome and vascular malformations; MRA provided additional information in children with sickle cell anemia, but not in children with headaches or seizures; and a normal MRI usually forecast a normal MRA, and vice versa.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of MRA as an adjunct to MRI in children with neurologic diseases.
the evaluation of the role of magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) in the assessment of children with neurologic conditions.
the use of MRA in a variety of pediatric neurological conditions, and its comparison to MRI.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MRI is the study of choice for most children with neurologic conditions.
MRI is still the primary imaging technique in the pediatric neuroimaging field and MRA is complementary to MRI in the diagnosis of vascular diseases.
MRA is a useful adjunct in the evaluation of the child with a suspected neurovascular disorder.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MRA is a useful tool in the evaluation of patients with neurologic disorders, particularly in the setting of known or suspected cerebral vasculopathy.
MRA is a useful adjunctive test to MRI in children with neurologic conditions.

MRA should be used to supplement the information gained from MRI in the evaluation of patients with known vascular disorders, but not as a substitute for MRI in the evaluation for other neurologic disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MRA is not a good screening test for children with neurologic problems.
the use of MRA is not indicated in all patients.

MRI should be performed first in children with neurologic conditions, and MRA should be performed only in those patients in whom the MRI is abnormal and in whom the MRI findings suggest an intracranial vascular abnormality.
